chunks: Scope triggers and how to use them. The question: What are triggers on a scope? How do I use them?
A trigger tells the scope when to start each sweep of the screen. Without one, every sweep starts at a random point in the signal, so a repeating waveform smears or scrolls.
With an edge trigger you pick a voltage level and a direction, rising or falling.
Each sweep then starts at exactly that crossing, so all sweeps line up and the picture holds still.
Imagine timing runners on a track, and you start a stopwatch each time one crosses the same marker, going the same way.
If you overlay all the laps, they line up neatly because each begins at the same place. If you started the stopwatch at random moments, the laps would not line up.
A trigger is that marker. A scope can also keep data from before the marker.
The sine crosses 0 volts going up at t = 0 and every 1 milliseconds after. A scope triggers at each such crossing, starts the sweep there, and so every sweep looks identical.
Note the falling crossings at 0. 5 milliseconds are ignored because the slope setting is rising.
Trigger level: the voltage the signal must cross to start a sweep. Slope: whether the crossing is rising or falling.
Auto, normal, single mode: auto always shows something, even without a trigger. Normal only updates when a real trigger happens. Single captures one event, then stops.
Holdoff: a pause after a trigger during which new triggers are ignored, useful for bursts of pulses. Pre-trigger: the part of the capture recorded before the trigger event.
Look at a 1 kilohertz sine wave. Set an edge trigger at 0 volts, rising. Each sweep begins when the signal crosses 0 volts going up, which happens every 1 milliseconds.
All the sweeps overlay, and you see a steady sine. Now debugging: a microcontroller resets now and then.
Trigger on the reset line falling, in single mode, and put the supply voltage on a second channel. Place the trigger late on the screen so most of it shows history.
Now you can see whether the supply dipped just before the reset. That is the whole idea.
"A trigger tells the scope when to start each sweep, so repeating signals line up and sit still.
For an edge trigger I pick the source, a level on the clean part of the edge, and a slope.
Auto mode always shows something, normal waits for the condition, single captures one event. Holdoff handles bursts.
For hard problems I use pulse-width, runt, timeout or serial triggers, and the pre-trigger history shows what led to the event."
